'''Guy Deutscher''' ({{Langx|he|גי דויטשר}}; 19 March 1936{{snd}}4 May 2024) was an Israeli experimental physicist who specialized in [[solid-state physics]], [[low-temperature physics]], and [[superconductivity]]. He was a Professor Emeritus of Physics at [[Tel Aviv University]].<ref name="death">{{Cite web |title=Guy Deutscher |url=https://carnetdujour.lefigaro.fr/deces/annonces/508155592/ |access-date=2024-05-24 |website=[[Le Figaro]] |language=Fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Prof. Guy Deutscher Late {{!}} Faculty of Exact Sciences Raymond & Beverly Sackler |url=https://en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il/profile/guyde |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kraemer |first=Susan |date=7 September 2011 |title=Tel Aviv University Invents 40-Times Better Electricity Transmission |url=http://www.greenprophet.com/2011/09/tel-aviv-university-invents-40-times-better-electricity-transmission/ |accessdate=8 September 2011 |work=Green Prophet}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Deutscher was born in Berlin, Germany in 1936. His family fled the Nazis in 1939, shortly before [[World War II]], and settled down (first illegally) in [[Paris]], France. In July 1942, he was arrested with his mother at the "[[Vel' d'Hiv Roundup|Vel d'Hiv" roundup]] (la rafle du vélodrome d'hiver). Still, luckily because his father was a French prisoner of war, he escaped the fate of most of the other detainees who were sent to their deaths mainly to [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]]. After the war, Deutscher completed his Baccalaureat at [[Lycée Henri-IV|Lycée Henri IV]] in 1953. In 1956, he passed the entrance exam and was accepted into the [[École nationale supérieure des mines de Paris]], from which he graduated in 1959 with a Diplome d'ingenieur Civil des Mines, specializing in [[metallurgy]]. After three years of military service, he joined the research group of [[Nobel Prize in Physics|Nobel]] Laureate [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]] at the university of [[Paris-Sud University|Paris-Sud]] (Orsay). The group was later known as the "Orsay group on superconductivity". It was nicknamed by [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes|de Gennes]] as the four "Musketeers" including Deutscher, E. Guyon, J.P. Burger, and A. Martiner.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pierre-Gilles de Gennes, 1932-2007 |url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/conferences/physbioworkshop/DeGennesObit2.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325162222/https://www.weizmann.ac.il/conferences/physbioworkshop/DeGennesObit2.pdf |archive-date=25 Mar 2019 |accessdate=25 March 2019 |work=Physics of Biological Matter, Research Workshop of the Israel Science Foundation, Safed Summer Workshop, 2–7 September 2007}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
After spending two years as a postdoc at [[Rutgers University]] (1967-8) in the group of Bernie Serin,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rutgers University Department of Physics and Astronomy |url=https://www.physics.rutgers.edu/dept/history/ |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=www.physics.rutgers.edu}}</ref> he returned to France. He was appointed as an associate professor at the University of Paris-Orsay (IUT). In 1971, Deutsche immigrated to Israel and joined the Department of Physics at [[Tel Aviv University]], where he spent his entire career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of the School |url=https://physics.tau.ac.il/physics/shcool_history |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=physics.tau.ac.il |language=en-US}}</ref> He developed a new direction of research on experimental [[low-temperature physics]], with particular emphasis on granular [[Superconductivity|superconductors]], disordered media, [[Metal–insulator transition|metal-insulator]] and superconductor-semiconductor transitions properties of thin [[Superconductivity|superconducting films]] and [[Josephson junctions]]. He made contributions to the understanding of vortex dynamics in superconductors and the development of superconducting devices. In addition, he worked on [[Granular material|granular]] and disordered materials with an emphasis on the phenomenon of [[Percolation threshold|percolation.]]<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bontemps |first1=N. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4TnsCAAAQBAJ |title=The Vortex State |last2=Bruynseraede |first2=Yvan |last3=Deutscher |first3=Guy |last4=Kapitulnik |first4=Aharon |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-011-0974-1 |language=en}}</ref>

Deutscher published over 300 scientific papers in leading journals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Guy Deutscher |url=https://scholar.google.co.il/citations?user=aBqGgfMAAAAJ&hl=en |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=scholar.google.co.il}}</ref> He supervised numerous graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Many of his students went on to hold prominent positions in academia and industry in Israel and abroad.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physics Tree - Guy Deutscher Family Tree |url=https://academictree.org/physics/tree.php?pid=244862&pnodecount=4&cnodecount=2&fontsize=1 |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=academictree.org}}</ref>

== Contributions to high-temperature superconductivity ==
Deutscher's expertise in granular and disordered materials proved invaluable when high-temperature superconductivity was discovered in the late 1980s. He co-authored one of the most cited papers in the field with [[K. Alex Müller]], the Nobel laureate who discovered the [[cuprate superconductor]]s. This paper explored the relationship between the unique properties of [[high-temperature superconductivity]] and the inherent disorder in these materials. Deutscher's insight into the short coherence length of cuprates led to the first accepted explanation for the low critical current in ceramic and [[polycrystalline]] samples of these materials.{{cn|date=June 2024}}

Deutscher's group also pioneered the use of Andreev reflections to study the electronic properties of [[High-temperature superconductivity|high-temperature superconductors]]. This technique allowed for the measurement of the [[Superconducting energy gap|superconducting gap]] and provided insights into the nature of the [[pseudogap]] in these materials.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Quantum Levitation Can Make Objects Float and Fly |url=https://www.thoughtco.com/quantum-levitation-and-how-does-it-work-2699356 |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=ThoughtCo |language=en}}</ref>
